newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hamburger recall not seen hurting beef demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hamburger recall not seen hurting beef demand.

text.p: Last week's recall of 1.2 million pounds of frozen ground beef on fears of bacteria contamination should not have a major impact on U.S. beef demand, meat industry analysts and retailers said on Monday.
Hudson Foods Inc, headquartered in Rogers, Arkansas, recalled the frozen beef patties because of possible contamination by a potentially deadly strain of E.coli bacteria.
U.S. Agriculture Department investigators were searching for the cause of any contamination.

"I think customers are really pretty saavy about food safety and safe handling and preparation procedures. They've really kind of taken it to heart," said Rita Simmer, spokeswoman for Supervalu Inc, parent company of Cub Foods.
"Ironically at our Cub Food Stores we have a fresh ground beef ad this week that just broke yesterday (Sunday) and according to a source, there they are selling like crazy," Simmer said.
Simmer said Supervalu does not buy beef from Hudson Foods.
In addition to 116 Cub Food stores in 13 states, Supervalu supplies 4,900 stores in 48 states through its distribution centers.
Reduced beef demand also was not noticed this weekend by another national food distributor, Topco Associates of Morton Grove, Illinois.
"If it does have any significant impact on beef demand, I don't expect it would be felt this fast," Topco meat commodity analyst Kevin Bost said of the Hudson Foods recall.
"There would be a gradual slowdown in sales and a reduction in orders....but it has been handled in a way that should not stir up any fear," Bost said.
"I think that it was pretty well explained that it was not a general contamination, it was a specific product that was labeled and had product codes, so, I really don't expect a backlash," Bost said.
The recall would have had greater impact on beef demand if roasts or steaks had been included instead of just ground beef, said Dale Benson, livestock analyst with Dean-Witter Reynolds in Chicago.

Still, the timing of the announcement was unfavorable for the beef industry because it came two weeks before the long Labor Day holiday weekend, when a lot of hamburgers usually are cooked at outdoor picnics and backyard barbecues, Benson said.
"If you get continued press for the next week, it could be very negative as far as retail clearance is over Labor Day weekend," Benson said.

Hudson Foods Chief Financial Officer Charles Jurgensmeyer told Reuters earlier on Monday that the company had not had any cancellations of customer orders for its meat products after the announcement of the recall.
